body.text: The Philippine Supreme Court issued two major decisions over the past two months that could affect not just the work of Congress but also the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and the candidates who may run in the 2028 national and local elections.

In September, the Court ruled that Congress is mandated by the 1987 Constitution to pass a bill prohibiting political dynasties. This month, the Court nullified some aspects of the previous national budget because the item on unprogrammed appropriations increased the president’s spending program.

A few powerful clans have long dominated Philippine politics, which has entrenched inequality and elite rule. After the fall of the Marcos dictatorship in 1986, framers of the new Constitution wanted to democratize political participation by banning political dynasties. But in the end, they left it to Congress to define what a political dynasty is and pass a law prohibiting them. This ultimately doomed the Constitutional intent to ban dynasties because the few families that dominated both houses of Congress would not legislate against their own interests.

Responding to the petition against the failure and refusal of Congress to pass a law banning political dynasties over the past 39 years, the Court unanimously ruled that this was a “grave abuse of discretion. It reminded legislators that the provision against dynasties “is not merely an aspiration but a constitutional command.” The Court acknowledged that it cannot compel a co-equal branch of government “to perform a discretionary act,” but it noted that the case is “highly exceptional” because of the grave abuse of discretion and “manifest injustice.”

There are pending bills on the abolition of dynasties, and even President Marcos has signaled his support for the measure. However, critics pointed out that the House version endorsed by the president’s son would merely regulate dynasties, and if passed into law, families like the Marcoses and the Dutertes can still field multiple candidates in several elective posts at the same time.

The release of the Court ruling was therefore timely since it can be used as a reference for legislators in finalizing the bill to end dynasties once and for all and allow a new breed of leaders a greater chance to serve in government.

Another landmark decision of the Court released this month was about the unprogrammed appropriations in the previous national budget. The Court ruled that these were unconstitutional because of Congress’s increase of the Special Road Fund, which resulted in an increase in the president’s total recommended appropriations. It added that there should be no lump sums in unprogrammed appropriations and that this budgetary item “needs clear limits and safeguards to preserve fiscal discipline, transparency, and accountability.”

Simply put, the Court reiterated its earlier ruling against the pork barrel system. Lump sum funds inserted by Congress or budget items that expanded the discretionary spending of the president are “constitutionally infirm” since they can be turned into a corruption-prone pork barrel distribution program.

Again, the Court ruling was timely, since the Senate will tackle the House-approved 2028 budget bill next month. It could become a point of contention between the two chambers, especially since most House members are reliant on pork barrel funds to boost their electoral chances. Meanwhile, the Marcos government has asked the Court for a partial reconsideration and clarification on some matters of the ruling pertaining to funds that have already been spent.

The budget ruling could revive the clamor for accountability since it validated the assertion of progressive lawmakers and anti-corruption watchdogs that the Marcos government has drafted a budget that institutionalized and expanded suspicious items in the unprogrammed appropriations.

Even Vice President Sara Duterte cited the Court decision to castigate Marcos for his role in enabling the rampant corruption in the bureaucracy. Duterte has no credibility to speak on this issue since she herself is embroiled in a corruption scandal, but her statement highlights how the ruling can spur the demand to hold the Marcos administration accountable for budget-related controversies.

The two Supreme Court rulings pose a challenge to the work of Congress, whose sessions will resume next month. The Senate can initially rework the budget bill before the review of the Bicameral Committee. But in the end, it is not just Congress that will be put in the spotlight but President Marcos, who has to persuade the public that he acted in good faith when he signed and implemented a budget law that contains unconstitutional provisions.
